ab_mount_temple_greenwood_locke.descent_text: Descend the Southwest Ridge, the walk-up line on the mountain, to Moraine Lake. It is the quickest way down and is shared with hikers, so the party finishes on the Moraine Lake road rather than back at Paradise Valley; a shuttle or ride between the two ends saves time.

bc_north_howser_tower_all_along_the_watc.approach: The usual way in is from the East Creek Basin camp. Hike up the ridge toward the middle tower and traverse a snow slope to the upper ridge overlooking the foot of the North Tower, then set rappels there to reach the glacier. Cross the cirque to the foot of the west face. Rockfall comes down both the rappels and the cirque from the face above, so move through quickly. Climbing begins on ledges over the glacier, at the point where the lower apron juts out farthest.
bc_north_howser_tower_all_along_the_watc.descent_text: From the summit ridge, rappel the east face. The stations vary between pins and slung horns and shift from year to year, so carry slings and extra cord. The face is loose, rockfall is a real hazard, and ropes snag easily. Below the bergschrund a short downclimb leads onto the glacier, and from there the party walks back toward the Applebee camp.

bc_north_howser_tower_the_seventh_rifle.approach: The approach is from the East Creek Basin. A common plan is to bivy at the boulder below Middle Howser, then rappel the bolted anchors to reach the foot of the tower. The line begins left of the west face's lowest point, where a broad crack in a corner sits beside a splitter hand crack on the wall to its right.
bc_north_howser_tower_the_seventh_rifle.descent_text: Rappel the east face just below the summit, working down to the bergschrund, then downclimb a short way onto the glacier. The east face is loose, so move with care, and carry spare webbing to replace old anchors. From the glacier, walk back to the Applebee camp.

bc_north_howser_tower_young_warrior.approach: This route is on the west face of North Howser Tower. One approach is from the East Creek Basin by rappelling down to the glacier, which is strenuous; a longer alternative skirts the north side of the massif. The base is on the west face.

ca_angel_wings_hell_on_wings.approach: Angel Wings is a backcountry wall in the Sequoia high country, reached from the Crescent Meadow trailhead near Moro Rock on a long walk in. Hamilton Lake is the closest and best camp for the wall. Hell on Wings climbs the south face pillar, following a crack system just left of the Rowell-Jones line.

ca_angel_wings_just_a_rock_in_the_park.approach: Angel Wings is a backcountry wall in the Sequoia high country, reached from the Crescent Meadow trailhead near Moro Rock on a long walk in. Hamilton Lake is the closest and best camp for the wall. The route starts in the middle of the main south face, at the left one of two ramps that cross to form an X a few hundred feet above the base.

ca_bubbs_creek_wall_crystal_bonsai.approach: Walk east from Roads End on the Bubbs Creek trail, the same approach as for Charlotte Dome, to the good campsites just past Charlotte Creek. Continue down the trail a short way until the long wall comes into view on the left. The route follows the longest section of the wall, just left of centre, along a white crystal band. It starts at a big pine just up and right of the huge white left-facing dihedral that marks the foot of that band.
ca_bubbs_creek_wall_crystal_bonsai.descent_text: Parties come off the top by heading west and down the Charlotte Creek drainage, toward Charlotte Dome.

ca_the_fortress_2_the_siege.approach: Start from the Paradise Ridge trailhead off Mineral King Road, close to Atwell Mill campground, and hike the trail up to the ridge. Leave the trail there and go cross-country north-northwest, contouring through small drainages until you can see the wall and the gully beneath it. Keep to the gully's east flank until you are below the wall, then cross over and climb to the base. The Siege takes the natural line up the middle of the face on the obvious crack.

nt_lotus_flower_tower_southeast_face_2.descent_text: Parties rappel the route. The upper part has fixed belay stations, so the rappels there follow the climb; keep the ropes clear of the knobs, which catch them. At the large bivy ledge the rappel line leaves the climbing line and runs down a bolted line on the face, to the right of the chimneys, as far as the top of the third pitch, with a further rappel from there to the top of the first. Do not rappel into the chimney, where ropes jam, and since the stations on the open face are hard to spot, note the anchors on the way up.

nu_north_tower_british_american_route_sc.approach: From the Summit Lake shelter, follow the Caribou Glacier northwest to the divide between the Caribou and Parade glaciers. Drop to the Parade Glacier either down the steep snow and ice by the west side of the divide or, on the east side, by rappelling from an anchor close to the saddle. The route begins just right of the big, deep gully above the Parade Glacier; after a heavy snow winter, begin from the right side of the molar-shaped snowfield. The far wall of that gully sheds rock, so do not stop beneath it.
nu_north_tower_british_american_route_sc.descent_text: Three ways down start from the summit plateau. The usual one crosses the plateau to an obvious rappel point, then rappels on doubled ropes into the gap separating the two towers, and continues down a rotten gully by more rappels to a snowfield. Cross that exposed, possibly icy snowfield to rock on its far side and rappel the slabs and cliffs below from established anchors. The alternative is to rappel the route, but only the upper part is equipped, so most of the anchors lower down would have to be built on a very big face before climbing out of the Parade Glacier.
